title: One qubit: from states to interference
outcome: Read a one-qubit state, obtain its Z-basis probabilities, tell a probability apart from a sampled frequency, apply X, H and Z, and explain how a relative sign changes what a later H does.
scope_note: These are foundation skills. Completing this chapter is not mastery of quantum algorithms.
notation_contract: A one-qubit state is written |psi> = a|0> + b|1> with amplitude vector (a, b). Circuit arrows are chronological: H -> Z means H first, then Z. Measurements are in the computational (Z) basis unless labelled otherwise. Every core example is an ideal, noiseless, single-qubit experiment. Qubit 0 is the top wire and the least significant bit.

topics.title: Bits, qubits, and the computational basis
topics.objective: Tell a state description apart from a measurement result, and read basis notation.
learning_objectives: Write |0> and |1> as the vectors (1,0) and (0,1).
Explain that the two entries are amplitudes for two outcomes, not two qubits.
Identify which panel shows a recorded classical result rather than a state.
topics.teach_markdown:
A classical bit holds one of two values, 0 or 1. In this laboratory a qubit is described using two reference states, written `|0>` and `|1>`. We represent them as the vectors `(1, 0)` and `(0, 1)`.

Those two entries are **amplitudes**, one for each measurement outcome. They are not two separate qubits. A single wire carries a single qubit, and the amplitude table beneath it always has one row per outcome.

A measurement produces a classical result, such as the digit 0. It does not print the vector. Keeping the *description* (the amplitude table) separate from the *result* (a recorded digit) is the habit this whole chapter depends on.

These two reference states are called the **computational basis**, and they are the starting point for describing every other qubit state you will meet.

topics.title: Amplitudes become probabilities
topics.objective: Calculate squared magnitudes and check normalization.
learning_objectives: Apply the Born rule P(0)=|a|^2 and P(1)=|b|^2.
Check that squared magnitudes sum to 1.
Explain why a negative amplitude does not produce a negative probability.
topics.teach_markdown:
For a state `a|0> + b|1>`, a Z-basis measurement gives outcome 0 with probability `|a|^2` and outcome 1 with probability `|b|^2`. This is the **Born rule**, and the quantity being squared is the *magnitude* of the amplitude.

A valid normalized state satisfies `|a|^2 + |b|^2 = 1`. That is what makes the two probabilities a complete distribution.

Amplitudes may be negative, and in general they are complex numbers. Probabilities never are. Squaring a magnitude removes the sign, which is why `(3/5, 4/5)` and `(-3/5, 4/5)` produce exactly the same probabilities. We start with real coefficients so the arithmetic stays visible; Chapter 2 introduces complex phases properly.

That hidden sign is not decoration. Later in this chapter you will build a circuit where it decides the final answer.

topics.title: Measurement, shots, and replay
topics.objective: Tell repeated preparation apart from repeated measurement of an already measured qubit.
learning_objectives: Describe the conditional state left behind by an ideal Z measurement.
Explain why a fresh shot restarts the preparation.
Read an observed frequency without confusing it with an exact probability.
topics.teach_markdown:
In an ideal projective Z measurement two things happen at once. An outcome is sampled using the state's probabilities, and the qubit is left in the basis state matching that outcome. That leftover state is called the **conditional state**.

So if you measure again straight away, with no gate in between, you get the same answer. Nothing is left to be random: the qubit is already sitting on `|0>` or `|1>`.

A **shot** is different. A shot throws the trajectory away and starts the whole preparation again from the beginning. Sixteen shots are sixteen independent preparations, each followed by one measurement.

That is why exact probabilities and observed counts are printed in separate panels. Equal probabilities do not require equal counts. More shots usually estimate the probabilities more closely, but one particular larger sample is not guaranteed to be closer than a smaller one.

**Replay** shows you a saved run again, including the outcomes it actually recorded. It is not a new measurement, and it does not undo one.

prediction.prompt: You will run 16 fresh preparations of |+>. Must the result be exactly eight zeros?

options.label: Yes, because the probabilities are exactly 1/2 each
No; exactly eight is possible but not required
No; eight zeros is impossible

steps.title: Sixteen fresh shots

steps.title: Two hundred and fifty-six shots
steps.instruction: Run 256 fresh shots and compare the observed frequency with the exact probability again.

steps.title: Replay
steps.instruction: Replay the saved run. The recorded samples do not change. A new run may differ.

topics.title: Read a circuit and use the X gate
topics.objective: Follow operation order and predict a basis-state flip.
learning_objectives: Read operations in chronological order along a wire.
Predict the effect of X on any amplitude vector.
Construct a circuit that meets a stated goal under published constraints.
topics.teach_markdown:
A circuit wire identifies one qubit, and the operations on it happen in the order they are drawn, left to right. Each gate acts on the state produced by everything before it.

The **X gate** exchanges the two amplitudes: `(a, b)` becomes `(b, a)`. On the basis states this swaps `|0>` and `|1>`, which is why it is often called a bit flip. On a general state it moves the amplitudes without changing their values.

Because swapping twice puts everything back, applying X twice returns the original state. Every gate in this chapter is reversible in that sense; measurement is the operation that is not, and it is shown separately.

topics.title: H and superposition
topics.objective: Understand H as a specific linear operation, not a randomizer.
learning_objectives: State what H does to |0>, |1>, |+> and |->.
Explain why H is deterministic even though measurement is not.
Reach a stated distribution goal with more than one valid circuit.
topics.teach_markdown:
The **Hadamard gate**, written H, maps `|0>` to `|+> = (|0> + |1>)/sqrt(2)` and `|1>` to `|-> = (|0> - |1>)/sqrt(2)`. Both results give equal Z-basis probabilities, so their probability bars look identical. Their amplitude tables do not: one has two plus signs, the other has a minus on the second entry.

H also maps `|+>` back to `|0>` and `|->` back to `|1>`. Applying H twice returns the input.

For a general state, H maps `(a, b)` to `((a+b)/sqrt(2), (a-b)/sqrt(2))`. That formula is the whole gate. It is an exact, deterministic, reversible operation.

This is worth saying plainly: **H is not a coin flip**. It always does the same thing to the same input. Randomness enters only when you measure a state whose outcome is genuinely uncertain. And a superposition is defined relative to a chosen basis. It is not a list of answers waiting to be printed.

prediction.prompt: Will two H gates necessarily leave the Z probabilities at 50/50?

options.label: Yes, because each H randomizes the qubit
No; from |0> two H gates return |0>, giving P(0)=1
Yes, but only for 256 shots or more
No; two H gates always give P(1)=1

steps.title: H on |0>
steps.instruction: Prepare |0>, place one H, and step forward. The amplitudes are both +1/sqrt(2) and the bars are 1/2 each.

steps.title: H on |1>

steps.title: H twice

topics.title: Z, relative phase, and global phase
topics.objective: Recognize a relative sign change without claiming that every minus sign is observable.
learning_objectives: Predict that Z leaves the immediate Z-basis probabilities unchanged.
Distinguish a relative phase between populated components from a global phase on the whole vector.
Explain why -|1> and |1> are the same physical state.
topics.teach_markdown:
The **Z gate** maps `(a, b)` to `(a, -b)`. It changes the sign of the second amplitude and nothing else. Because magnitudes are unchanged, the **immediate** Z-basis probabilities are unchanged too.

On `|+>` this produces `|->`. Those are genuinely different states: the sign between two populated components is a **relative phase**, and a later gate can turn it into a difference you can measure.

On `|1>` the story is different. `Z|1> = -|1>`, and that minus multiplies the entire state vector. A factor that multiplies *every* amplitude is a **global phase**, and it changes no prediction about that state at all. `|1>` and `-|1>` describe the same physical situation.

So the question to ask is never just "is there a minus sign?" It is: **did one populated component change sign, or did the whole vector?**

One caution for later chapters: do not turn "global phase is unobservable" into a rule that phases can always be dropped. A phase that becomes conditional inside a controlled operation is a relative phase in the larger system. Chapter 4 returns to this.

sources.title: Limitations on quantum information (global phase) - IBM Quantum Learning

topics.title: Interference: why H-H and H-Z-H differ
topics.objective: Add amplitudes before squaring, and locate the step at which the probabilities first differ.
learning_objectives: Apply H to a general amplitude vector by adding and subtracting contributions.
Identify the step where two circuits first differ in Z probabilities.
Explain why an inserted measurement destroys the interference.
topics.teach_markdown:
This is the topic the rest of the chapter was building towards.

H maps `(a, b)` to `((a+b)/sqrt(2), (a-b)/sqrt(2))`. Each output amplitude is a **sum of contributions** from both input amplitudes. Signs matter in that sum, because contributions can add or cancel. Only after the sum is complete do you square to get a probability.

Start from `|0>` and write `a = 1/sqrt(2)`.

| Circuit | After first H | After optional Z | After final H | Final P(1) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H -> H | (a, a) | (a, a) | (1, 0) | 0 |
| H -> Z -> H | (a, a) | (a, -a) | (0, 1) | 1 |

Follow the second row. Into output 0 go the contributions +1/2 and -1/2, which cancel. Into output 1 go +1/2 and +1/2, which add. The first row is the same arithmetic with the signs the other way round.

So the two circuits have **identical** probabilities right up until the final H. The Z gate changed only a sign, and a sign is invisible in a probability bar. The last H is what converts that sign into a difference in the outcome.

Those arrows are **amplitude contributions**, not paths a particle travels.

**If you measure in the middle instead**, the interference is gone. Compare H -> H with H -> Measure -> H. The measured qubit lands on `|0>` or `|1>`, and either branch followed by H gives equal final probabilities. Inspecting a saved simulator snapshot does not perform this measurement; only an actual measurement operation in the circuit does.

After their final H gate
After the first H gate

H maps (a, b) to ((a+b)/sqrt(2), (a-b)/sqrt(2)). Apply that formula to (a, -a) with a = 1/sqrt(2).

Worked answer: from |0>, H gives (a, a) and Z gives (a, -a). The final H sends (a, -a) to (0, 1) = |1>, so P(1)=1. Without the Z, the final H sends (a, a) to (1, 0) = |0>. From |1> the chain is |1> -> |-> -> |+> -> |0>.

topics.title: Build, explain, and revisit the mystery
topics.objective: Combine the chapter's skills in a new task and connect them back to the search preview.
learning_objectives: Control a circuit's output by choosing one operation.
Explain a changed result from an amplitude trace.
Separate exact probabilities from observed counts in your own run.
Connect relative phase to the Grover oracle step you saw earlier.
topics.teach_markdown:
Three short capstones, then a return to the experiment you started with.

You now have everything needed to control a one-qubit circuit deliberately: you can read a state, convert amplitudes to probabilities, apply X, H and Z, tell a relative phase from a global one, and predict where interference will show up.

The last part matters most. When you first ran the search preview, the oracle changed a sign and **no probability bar moved**. That looked like nothing happening. You now know exactly what kind of event that was, and what has to come next for it to matter.

Four
None; the middle slot cannot change the outcome

tasks.prompt: Same fixed H gates. Fill the middle slot so the final state is |1>.

tasks.title: Capstone A, part 3: the role of the middle slot
tasks.prompt: What does the middle operation actually do in this circuit?

options.label: It sets the relative sign between the two amplitudes, which the final H turns into a definite outcome
It randomly selects which outcome the measurement reports
It changes the probabilities immediately, before the final H
It has no effect unless more shots are used

tasks.title: Capstone B: diagnose the changed input
tasks.prompt: The circuit H -> Z -> H now starts from |1>. Which trace and result are correct?

options.label: |1> -> |-> -> |+> -> |0>, so the outcome is 0
|1> -> |+> -> |-> -> |1>, so the outcome is 1
|1> -> |-> -> |-> -> |1>, so the outcome is 1
The result is 50/50 because the input changed

free_text.prompt: Optional: explain in your own words why changing the input changed the result. This box receives feedback only and is not graded.

tasks.title: Capstone C: separate theory and observation
tasks.prompt: Using your own H-only run, report the exact probability of outcome 0, the measured count of outcome 0, and the shot total. Then select why the counts need not split equally.

options.label: Each shot is an independent random trial, so a finite sample scatters around the expected value
The simulator is imprecise
The exact probabilities are not really 1/2
Counts always split equally once there are at least 256 shots

tasks.title: Revisit: your first Grover mystery
tasks.prompt: In your saved N=4 search run, the oracle changed a sign and no probability bar moved. Which idea from this chapter explains why that sign can still matter?

options.label: A relative phase changes nothing immediately, but a later operation can turn it into different probabilities
The oracle secretly increased the target's probability straight away
A global phase on the whole state became measurable
More shots would have revealed the change at the oracle step

hints.text: Use your H-H against H-Z-H comparison from Topic 1.7.
Inspect the state immediately before the last H in each version.
An empty middle slot leaves (a, a); a Z makes it (a, -a). The final H sends the first to |0> and the second to |1>.

Worked answer: empty slot gives |0>, Z gives |1>. From |1> the chain H -> Z -> H runs |1> -> |-> -> |+> -> |0>. After a revealed answer the laboratory offers an equivalent new-input task before recording independent evidence.

revisit.status_explanation: Completing one foundation chapter does not earn Can Explain or Mastered for Grover. Those require the algorithm's own objectives, in Chapter 6.

recap: A number from 0 to 1; all mutually exclusive outcomes sum to 1.
A sequence of instructions read in execution order.
An observed result; several samples need not exactly match the predicted proportions.
